Which of the following statements is correct under the Specific Relief Act, 1963 ?

options.label: A
options.text: The injunction may be granted to enforce the negative covenant.

options.label: B
options.text: The injunction must be refused because contracts of personal service cannot be enforced.

options.label: C
options.text: The court must compel Ajeet Singh to sing for Yash Aditya Music Company.

options.label: D
options.text: Only damages can be granted.

rectification.principle: Under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 (Lumley v. Wagner / Niranjan Shankar Golikari), even though the affirmative promise of personal service cannot be specifically enforced, the court may grant an injunction to enforce the negative agreement not to perform for rivals during the contract term.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates stop at Section 14(c) / 41(e) ('no specific performance of personal service') and forget the express exception in Section 42.
rectification.howToRectify: Section 42 SRA = Injunction to perform negative agreement even when affirmative personal service cannot be compelled.

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure (BNSS / CrPC)
questions.question: Under Section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1973, 'Default Bail' (or statutory bail) is a right of the accused if the investigation is not completed :

options.label: A
options.text: After a fixed period of 30 days for all types of offences.

options.label: B
options.text: Upon the expiry of 120 days specifically for offences against the State.

options.label: C
options.text: After 60 days or 90 days, contingent upon the maximum punishment prescribed for the offence.

options.label: D
options.text: Immediately following the completion of the initial 15-day police custody.

rectification.principle: Section 167(2)(a) CrPC grants indefeasible default bail if charge-sheet is not filed within 90 days (death, life imprisonment, or >=10 years) or 60 days (all other offences).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Special statutes like NDPS (180 days) have different limits, whereas CrPC 167(2) uses the 60/90-day split.
rectification.howToRectify: CrPC Sec. 167(2): 90 days (>=10 yrs/life/death) | 60 days (others).

questions.subject: Environmental Law
questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India forms the primary legislative basis for the Parliament enacting the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 ?

options.label: A
options.text: Article 252

options.label: B
options.text: Article 233

options.label: C
options.text: Article 253

options.label: D
options.text: None of the above

rectification.principle: The Preamble of the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 expressly states it was enacted to implement decisions taken at the 1972 UN Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment—invoking Parliament's treaty-implementation power under Article 253.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: The Water Act, 1974 was enacted under Article 252 (State resolutions), whereas the Air Act, 1981 and EPA, 1986 were enacted under Article 253!
rectification.howToRectify: Water Act 1974 = Art. 252 (State resolutions); Air Act 1981 & EPA 1986 = Art. 253 (Stockholm Conference).

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: Under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, what condition applies for appointing a guardian for a married female minor ?

options.label: A
options.text: The husband must be declared legally incompetent

options.label: B
options.text: The husband must be considered unfit by the Court

options.label: C
options.text: The parents must apply jointly for such appointment

options.label: D
options.text: The husband must consent to such appointment

rectification.principle: Section 19(a) of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 prohibits a court from appointing a guardian of the person of a minor who is a married female and whose husband is not, in the opinion of the Court, unfit to be guardian of her person.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates guess consent or formal incompetency declaration instead of the exact statutory phrase 'unfit in the opinion of the Court'.
rectification.howToRectify: Section 19(a) GWA: Guardian for married female minor ONLY if husband is unfit in the Court's opinion.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: Under the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, within how many months from the date of marriage must dowry received before marriage be transferred to the woman ?

options.label: A
options.text: Within six months

options.label: B
options.text: Within seven months

options.label: C
options.text: Within three months

options.label: D
options.text: Within five months

rectification.principle: Under Section 6(1)(a) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, any dowry received by any person other than the woman must be transferred to her within 3 months after the date of marriage (if received before marriage) or 3 months after receipt.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Numeric periods under Section 6 (3 months to transfer vs 6 months to 2 years imprisonment for failure) get conflated.
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 6(1): 3 months to transfer dowry to the woman (trustee duty).

questions.subject: Taxation Law
questions.question: An assessee pays a medical insurance premium for himself and his family and claims a deduction while computing total income. What is the correct position under the Income Tax Act, 1961 ?

options.label: A
options.text: Deduction is not permitted in such cases

options.label: B
options.text: Deduction is allowed subject to prescribed limits and conditions

options.label: C
options.text: Deduction is allowed without any monetary limit

options.label: D
options.text: Deduction is allowed only for senior citizens

rectification.principle: Section 80D of the Income-tax Act, 1961 allows deduction for health insurance premiums paid (other than by cash) for self, spouse, dependent children, and parents, subject to statutory caps (Rs. 25,000 / Rs. 50,000 for senior citizens).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Straightforward if you connect medical insurance premium to Section 80D.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: Sec. 80C = Life insurance/PPF; Sec. 80D = Medical/Health insurance.

questions.subject: Criminal Law (BNS / IPC)
questions.question: Under the Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860, in which of the following scenarios does the "Right of Private Defence of the Body" extend to the extent of voluntarily causing death to the assailant ?

options.label: A
options.text: A simple assault committed without the use of a weapon

options.label: B
options.text: A case of theft where the value of the stolen property exceeds ₹ 10,000

options.label: C
options.text: An assault committed with the specific intention of kidnapping or abducting a person

options.label: D
options.text: An act of criminal trespass occurring on open, vacant land

rectification.principle: Section 100 IPC (Sec. 38 BNS) lists 7 situations where private defence of body extends to causing death, including Clause Fifthly: 'An assault with the intention of kidnapping or abducting'.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Theft and criminal trespass concern property (Sec. 103 IPC), not body (Sec. 100 IPC), and simple theft does not allow causing death.
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize all 7 clauses of Sec. 100 IPC: Death, Grievous hurt, Rape, Unnatural lust, Kidnapping/Abducting, Wrongful confinement, Acid throwing.

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure (BNSS / CrPC)
questions.question: Under Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, if a police officer-in-charge determines that an investigation is not warranted because the case lacks sufficient gravity, they are legally obligated to notify the informant of this decision within :

options.label: A
options.text: 24 hours

options.label: B
options.text: 14 days

options.label: C
options.text: 7 days

options.label: D
options.text: 30 days

rectification.principle: Under Section 173(3) / 176(2) BNSS, 2023, where preliminary inquiry or refusal of investigation occurs (or where officer decides not to investigate under Sec. 176(1)(b)), the police officer must notify the informant within 14 days (specifically under the BNSS 14-day timeline for preliminary inquiry/report).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Old CrPC Section 157(2) required notifying the informant 'forthwith' without a fixed day count; BNSS introduced the 14-day period.
rectification.howToRectify: Note BNSS Sec. 173(3): 14 days timeline for preliminary inquiry / notifying informant.

questions.subject: Law of Contract & Specific Relief
questions.question:
X takes a loan of ₹ 10,00,000 from Bank A. Y signs a contract as surety, promising to pay the bank if X defaults. After 3 months, Bank A agrees to reduce the interest rate and extends the repayment period by 6 months without informing Y. Subsequently, X defaults on the loan.

Which of the following statements correctly describes Y's liability under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 ?

options.label: A
options.text: Y is partially discharged from liability because Bank A's modification increased the risk to Y without his consent.

options.label: B
options.text: Y is fully liable for the entire loan because a surety is always liable once the principal debtor defaults.

options.label: C
options.text: Y is not liable at all because the principal debtor defaulted after the contract modification.

options.label: D
options.text: Y is liable only if the bank sues the principal debtor first, regardless of the modification.

rectification.principle: Under Sections 133 and 135 of the Indian Contract Act, variance in terms or giving time without the surety's consent discharges the surety as to transactions subsequent to the variance (note: the Official Final Key for AIBE-XXI Set A records Option A as the official answer).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Section 133 discharges surety for transactions subsequent to variance (often framed as 'not liable at all' in single-loan contracts), whereas the BCI Final Key selected Option A.
rectification.howToRectify: Review Sections 133, 134, and 135 ICA carefully: unauthorized variance/extension discharges the surety for subsequent liability.

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.question: Which of the following does not fall under the framework of presumption under Section 2 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 ?

options.label: A
options.text: Conclusive proof

options.label: B
options.text: Shall presume

options.label: C
options.text: Unassailable proof

options.label: D
options.text: May be

rectification.principle: Section 2(1)(c), (h), and (l) of BSA 2023 (mirroring Sec. 4 IEA) define three categories: 'May presume', 'Shall presume', and 'Conclusive proof'. 'Unassailable proof' is not a statutory term.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: 'Unassailable proof' sounds like a synonym for conclusive proof, and 'May be' (minor typo for 'May presume') distracts readers.
rectification.howToRectify: Stick strictly to the three statutory terms in Sec. 2 BSA: May presume, Shall presume, Conclusive proof.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.statuteRef: Constitution of India (Art. 21 - Right to Privacy)
questions.question:
Directions : The following question consists of two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). You are to examine these two statements carefully and decide if the Assertion (A) and the Reason (R) are individually true and if so, whether the Reason (R) is a correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

Assertion (A) : The right to privacy has been judicially recognised as an integral part of Article 21 of the Constitution of India.

Reason (R) : Privacy is expressly enumerated as a separate Fundamental Right in Part III of the Constitution of India.

In the context of the Constitution of India and the decision in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1, which one of the following is correct ?

options.label: A
options.text: (A) is false, but (R) is true.

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: C
options.text: (A) is true, but (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

rectification.principle: In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017), a 9-judge bench unanimously held that the right to privacy is an intrinsic, implied part of Article 21 and Part III—it is NOT expressly enumerated as a standalone article in Part III.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Because privacy is a Fundamental Right post-Puttaswamy, candidates mistakenly assume it is expressly written in Part III.
rectification.howToRectify: Puttaswamy = Implicit/intrinsic right under Art. 21, not an expressly named separate article.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.statuteRef: Constitution of India (Art. 248 & Entry 97 List I)
questions.question: Under the scheme of distribution of legislative powers in the Constitution of India, a subject which is not enumerated in either the State List or the Concurrent List falls within the residuary field of legislation. Such residuary power is vested in :

options.label: A
options.text: The State Legislatures

options.label: B
options.text: The Parliament

options.label: C
options.text: The President of India

options.label: D
options.text: The Supreme Court of India

rectification.principle: Article 248 read with Entry 97 of the Union List (Seventh Schedule) vests exclusive residuary power of legislation in Parliament.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Under the Government of India Act, 1935, residuary power vested in the Governor-General; India's Constitution shifted it to Parliament.
rectification.howToRectify: Art. 248 + Entry 97 List I = Exclusive residuary power of Parliament.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: "The rules of natural justice were not confined to the narrow precincts of the prevailing definition of quasi-judicial functions." This principle was laid down in which case ?

options.label: A
options.text: Ridge v. Baldwin (1964) A.C. 40

options.label: B
options.text: Conway v. Rimmer (1968) A.C. 910

options.label: C
options.text: Maradana Mosque Trustees v. Mahmud (1967) (1) A.C. 13

options.label: D
options.text: A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India AIR 1970 SC 150

rectification.principle: Ridge v. Baldwin (1964) is the landmark House of Lords decision that dismantled the old distinction between judicial/quasi-judicial and administrative acts, extending natural justice whenever rights are affected (followed in India in A.K. Kraipak).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: A.K. Kraipak (1970) applied the exact same principle in India, making Option D a strong distractor.
rectification.howToRectify: First laid down: Ridge v. Baldwin (1964); Indian adoption: A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India (1970).

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: "Administrative law is the law concerning the powers and procedures of administrative agencies, including especially the law governing judicial review of administrative action." This definition was given by :

options.label: A
options.text: Ivor Jennings

options.label: B
options.text: K.C. Davis

options.label: C
options.text: A.V. Dicey

options.label: D
options.text: H.W.R. Wade

rectification.principle: Kenneth Culp Davis (K.C. Davis) gave this classic agency-and-judicial-review definition in his Administrative Law Treatise.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Ivor Jennings and H.W.R. Wade also gave widely cited textbook definitions of Administrative Law.
rectification.howToRectify: Keyword cue: 'powers and procedures of administrative agencies' = K.C. Davis.

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.question: The five Golden Principles with respect to Circumstantial Evidence were laid down in which Supreme Court Judgment ?

options.label: A
options.text: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra, 1984 AIR 1622

options.label: B
options.text: Dudh Nath Pandey v. State of U.P., 1981 SCC (2) 166

options.label: C
options.text: Vasa Chandrasekhar Rao v. Ponna Satyanarayana & Anr., 2000 AIR SC 2138

options.label: D
options.text: Dr. Sunil Clifford Daniel v. State of Punjab (2012) 11 SCC 205

rectification.principle: In Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984), Justice Fazal Ali formulated the 'panchsheel' (five golden principles) of circumstantial evidence.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Subsequent circumstantial evidence judgments often quote Sharad Birdhichand Sarda, creating citation confusion.
rectification.howToRectify: Panchsheel / Five Golden Principles of circumstantial evidence = Sharad Birdhichand Sarda (1984).

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.question: According to Section 20 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, where the parties have not agreed on the place of arbitration, the arbitral tribunal shall determine it having regard to :

options.label: A
options.text: Place where the contract was executed.

options.label: B
options.text: Circumstances of the case, including the convenience of the parties.

options.label: C
options.text: Jurisdiction of the civil court alone.

options.label: D
options.text: Location of subject matter of dispute.

rectification.principle: Section 20(2) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 states that failing party agreement, the place of arbitration shall be determined by the arbitral tribunal having regard to the circumstances of the case, including the convenience of the parties.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates import Section 20 CPC (cause of action / defendant residence) into Section 20 of the Arbitration Act.
rectification.howToRectify: Section 20(2) A&C Act = Circumstances of the case + convenience of the parties.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: Under the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, what is the minimum term of imprisonment prescribed for giving or taking dowry ?

options.label: A
options.text: Not less than ten years

options.label: B
options.text: Not less than five years

options.label: C
options.text: Not less than three years

options.label: D
options.text: Not less than seven years

rectification.principle: Section 3(1) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 prescribes imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than 5 years, plus fine not less than Rs. 15,000 or the value of such dowry, whichever is more.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Section 304B IPC (Dowry Death) prescribes a 7-year minimum, whereas Section 3 Dowry Prohibition Act prescribes 5 years.
rectification.howToRectify: Dowry giving/taking (Sec. 3 DPA) = minimum 5 years; Dowry Death (Sec. 304B IPC / Sec. 80 BNS) = minimum 7 years.

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.statuteRef: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Order IX Rule 13)
questions.question:
Directions : The following question consists of two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). You are to examine these two statements carefully and decide if the Assertion (A) and the Reason (R) are individually true and if so, whether the Reason (R) is a correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

Assertion (A) : An ex parte decree may be set aside if the defendant satisfies the court that he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called for hearing.

Reason (R) : Under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the court must be satisfied that the summons was not duly served or that the defendant was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called for hearing.

Mark your answer as :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: (A) is true, but (R) is false.

options.label: C
options.text: (A) is false, but (R) is true.

options.label: D
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

rectification.principle: Order IX Rule 13 CPC sets out the two statutory grounds for setting aside an ex-parte decree: (1) summons was not duly served, or (2) defendant was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Verify that Reason (R) directly states the statutory rule explaining Assertion (A).
rectification.howToRectify: Order IX Rule 13 CPC = Not duly served OR sufficient cause for non-appearance.

questions.subject: Criminal Law (BNS / IPC)
questions.question: Under which specific provision of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, has the definition of a 'Terrorist Act' been formally integrated into India's general penal legislation for the first time ?

options.label: A
options.text: Section 152

options.label: B
options.text: Section 109

options.label: C
options.text: Section 113

options.label: D
options.text: Section 121

rectification.principle: Section 113 BNS defines 'Terrorist act' within the general penal code (alongside Sec. 111 Organized Crime and Sec. 112 Petty Organized Crime). Section 152 covers acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates mix up Sec. 111 (Organized Crime), Sec. 113 (Terrorist Act), and Sec. 152 (Sovereignty/Integrity).
rectification.howToRectify: BNS Chapter VI cluster: Sec. 111 = Organized crime; Sec. 112 = Petty organized crime; Sec. 113 = Terrorist act.

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure (BNSS / CrPC)
questions.question: According to the provisions of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, an accused person intending to apply for 'Plea Bargaining' must do so within how many days following the formal framing of charges ?

options.label: A
options.text: 7 days

options.label: B
options.text: 15 days

options.label: C
options.text: 60 days

options.label: D
options.text: 30 days

rectification.principle: Section 290(1) BNSS introduces a new 30-day limitation from the date of framing of charge for filing an application for plea bargaining (replacing the open-ended CrPC Sec. 265B).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: CrPC Sec. 265B had no 30-day cap, so candidates unfamiliar with BNSS Sec. 290 guess 15 or 60 days.
rectification.howToRectify: BNSS Sec. 290 Plea Bargaining = apply within 30 days from framing of charge.

questions.subject: Taxation Law
questions.question:
Directions : The following question consists of two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). You are to examine these two statements carefully and decide if the Assertion (A) and the Reason (R) are individually true and if so, whether the Reason (R) is a correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

Assertion (A) : Income-tax is levied on the total income of a person for the previous year.

Reason (R) : Income earned during the previous year is assessed to tax in the immediately succeeding assessment year under the Income-tax Act, 1961.

Mark answer as :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: (A) is false, but (R) is true.

options.label: C
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: D
options.text: (A) is true, but (R) is false.

rectification.principle: Under Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, income-tax is charged in respect of the total income of the 'previous year', and assessed in the 'assessment year' immediately following (subject to statutory exceptions like Sec. 172/174).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Verify carefully which option letter maps to 'Both true and R is correct explanation'—here it is Option C (not B or D).
rectification.howToRectify: Always read the option labels carefully in Assertion-Reason questions; the order of options changes across questions!

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.question: Which of the following is not stated in Section 63(4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, with regard to a certificate to verify the authenticity of electronic evidence ?

options.label: A
options.text: Signed by both the person in charge of the computer or communication device and an expert, with the certificate adhering to the format prescribed in the Adhiniyam's Schedule.

options.label: B
options.text: The form specified in the Schedule requires that electronic evidence be accompanied by a 'hash value'.

options.label: C
options.text: Qualification of an expert.

options.label: D
options.text: None of the above

rectification.principle: Section 63(4) BSA requires the certificate (in the Schedule format with hash value) to be signed by the person in charge of the device and an expert, but Section 63(4) itself does not specify the qualification of the expert.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates think 'None of the above' because Section 63 mentions 'an expert', overlooking that his qualifications are not prescribed in Sec. 63(4).
rectification.howToRectify: Check Sec. 63(4) BSA vs Schedule Part A & Part B: dual signature + hash value are stated; expert qualification is not stated.

questions.subject: Motor Vehicles Law
questions.question: A mandatory PUC Certificate is provided under which Section and Rule ?

options.label: A
options.text: Section 120(3) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and Rules 122 and 123 of the Centre Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989

options.label: B
options.text: Section 190(2) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and Rules 115 and 116 of the Centre Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989

options.label: C
options.text: Section 160(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and Rules 109 and 110 of the Centre Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989

options.label: D
options.text: Section 177(3) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and Rules 117 and 118 of the Centre Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989

rectification.principle: Rule 115(7) & Rule 116 of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 mandate a valid Pollution Under Control (PUC) certificate, and driving in violation of emission standards is punishable under Section 190(2) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Exact Rule numbers in CMVR 1989 require targeted revision.
rectification.howToRectify: Pair PUC Certificate with Section 190(2) MV Act + CMVR Rules 115 & 116.

questions.subject: Intellectual Property Law
questions.question: Under the Patents Act, 1970, a patent is granted to an inventor in India. Which of the following correctly reflects a limitation on the patentee's rights under the law ?

options.label: A
options.text: The patentee loses all rights once the invention is used by the Government

options.label: B
options.text: The Government may use the invention for its own purposes without the consent of the patentee

options.label: C
options.text: The invention cannot be used by the Government without permission

options.label: D
options.text: The patent becomes void if used by a government authority

rectification.principle: Section 47(1) (condition of grant) and Section 100 of the Patents Act, 1970 empower the Central Government and authorized persons to make, use, or exercise a patented invention for the purposes of Government without the patentee's consent (subject to royalty/compensation rules under Sec. 100).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates think patent exclusivity bars the State itself, whereas Section 47 expressly subjects every patent grant to government use.
rectification.howToRectify: Read Section 47 & Section 100 Patents Act, 1970: Sovereign/Government use is an inbuilt statutory limitation.

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.question: What do you mean by 'onus probandi' ?

options.label: A
options.text: 'Burden of proof' which places the responsibility on the party making an affirmative claim to substantiate it with evidence.

options.label: B
options.text: "The fact to be proved" or the "ultimate fact" that needs to be established in a legal case, such as the core elements of a crime or a cause of action.

options.label: C
options.text: The prosecution in a criminal case must prove beyond a reasonable doubt, not only a criminal act, but also a certain level of a guilty mind (mens rea), specified in the criminal statute.

options.label: D
options.text: Actual evidence, documents, or witnesses presented to substantiate that claim.

rectification.principle: Onus probandi literally means 'burden of proof'—reflecting the maxim ei incumbit probatio qui dicit, non qui negat (the burden lies on the party making the affirmative assertion).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Option B defines 'factum probandum' (the fact to be proved), which sounds similar to 'onus probandi'.
rectification.howToRectify: Distinguish: Onus probandi = Burden of proof; Factum probandum = Fact to be proved; Factum probans = Evidentiary fact.

questions.subject: Company Law
questions.question:
In the following question, a Statement is followed by two Conclusions, I and II.

Statement : Allegations have been made by the Minority Shareholders that ABC's promoters sold the optionally convertible preference shares and redeemable preference shares to a trust controlled by ABC's promoters at prices significantly below their fair market value, thereby causing a financial loss to ABC and its shareholders. What is the recourse for minority shareholders under law ?

Conclusion I : The Minority Shareholders can file for class action under Section 245 of the Companies Act, 2013, seeking directions from NCLT to either reverse the sale of optionally convertible preference shares and redeemable preference shares or to compensate the Minority Shareholders.

Conclusion II : The aggrieved members may proceed individually to protect their rights against acts of oppression or mismanagement under Section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013.

In the context of the above Statement and Conclusions, which one of the following is correct ?

options.label: A
options.text: Neither Conclusion I nor II follows

options.label: B
options.text: Both Conclusions I and II follow

options.label: C
options.text: Only Conclusion II follows

options.label: D
options.text: Only Conclusion I follows

rectification.principle: Both Section 245 (Class Action before NCLT seeking damages/compensation or restraining/reversing prejudicial acts) and Section 241 (Oppression and Mismanagement relief by members) are available statutory remedies under Chapter XVI of the Companies Act, 2013.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates note the numerical eligibility threshold under Section 244 for Section 241 and doubt individual recourse, overlooking that Section 244 permits waiver and individual/member petitioning.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember Chapter XVI Companies Act 2013: Sec. 241 (Oppression/Mismanagement) + Sec. 245 (Class Action).

questions.subject: Taxation Law
questions.question: According to Section 56(2)(x), of the Income-tax Act, 1961, if an individual receives a sum of money, without consideration, from a person other than a relative, and the amount exceeds the prescribed limit. What is the correct legal position ?

options.label: A
options.text: It is fully exempt from tax.

options.label: B
options.text: It is taxable only if received in cash.

options.label: C
options.text: It is treated as a capital receipt and is not taxable.

options.label: D
options.text: It is taxable under the head 'Income from Other Sources'.

rectification.principle: Under Section 56(2)(x) of the Income-tax Act, any aggregate sum of money exceeding Rs. 50,000 received without consideration from a non-relative (outside specified exceptions like marriage/inheritance) is taxable under 'Income from Other Sources'.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates think gifts are non-taxable capital receipts regardless of Section 56(2)(x).
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 56(2)(x): Non-relative gifts > Rs. 50,000 -> Income from Other Sources.

questions.subject: Intellectual Property Law
questions.question:
Read the following statements and choose the correct option.

Under the Copyright Act, 1957 :

Statement I : In the case of a posthumous literary work, copyright subsists for sixty years from the beginning of the calendar year next following the year in which the work is first published.

Statement II : For such works, publication refers to making the work available to the public by issue of copies or by communication to the public.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Statements I and II are false

options.label: B
options.text: Only Statement II is true

options.label: C
options.text: Both Statements I and II are true

options.label: D
options.text: Only Statement I is true

rectification.principle: Section 24(1) of the Copyright Act, 1957 grants 60 years from the calendar year next following first publication for posthumous works, and Section 3 defines 'publication' as making a work available to the public by issue of copies or by communicating the work to the public.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates recall the general 'life + 60 years' rule (Sec. 22) and forget the special posthumous-work rule in Section 24.
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 22 = Author's life + 60 yrs; Sec. 24 (Posthumous) = 60 yrs from year following first publication.

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.question: Which of the following statements is not true with respect to Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 ?

options.label: A
options.text: The requirement of a certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 ("Evidence Act"), is a condition precedent to the admissibility of an electronic record in evidence.

options.label: B
options.text: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal, (2020) 7 SCC 1 – landmark judgment stands as the latest interpretation of the relevant provisions, offering a consistent approach in line with the legislative intent.

options.label: C
options.text: In P.V. Anvar v. P.K. Basheer, the court held that Section 65B is a "complete code" for electronic evidence.

options.label: D
options.text: In State (NCT of Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu, reported in AIR 2005 SC 3820, the Hon'ble Supreme Court had held that courts could admit electronic records such as printouts and compact discs (CDs) as prima facie evidence without authentication.

rectification.principle: In Navjot Sandhu (2005), the Court allowed secondary electronic evidence via Sec. 63/65 without a Sec. 65B(4) certificate (later overruled by P.V. Anvar and Arjun Panditrao), NOT 'as prima facie evidence without authentication'; furthermore Navjot Sandhu is no longer good law.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: All four options cite real Section 65B cases, so you must spot the legal inaccuracy in Option D.
rectification.howToRectify: Trace the Section 65B timeline: Navjot Sandhu (overruled) -> Anvar v. Basheer (complete code) -> Arjun Panditrao (2020, Sec. 65B(4) mandatory for secondary electronic records).

questions.subject: Labour & Industrial Laws
questions.question: Which of the following is not included in "The Industrial Relations Code, 2020" ?

options.label: A
options.text: Trade Unions Act, 1926

options.label: B
options.text: Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 (IDR Act)

options.label: C
options.text: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947

options.label: D
options.text: Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946

rectification.principle: The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 amalgamated and repealed three central labour statutes: (1) Trade Unions Act, 1926, (2) Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, and (3) Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The IDR Act, 1951 is not part of it.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: The word 'Industries' in IDR Act makes it sound like an industrial relations statute.
rectification.howToRectify: IR Code 2020 = Trade Unions (1926) + Standing Orders (1946) + Industrial Disputes (1947).

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.question: Which of the following is not a document as per the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 ?

options.label: A
options.text: Caricature

options.label: B
options.text: Map

options.label: C
options.text: Inscription

options.label: D
options.text: Private papers

rectification.principle: Under the illustrations to Section 2(1)(d) of BSA 2023 (mirroring Sec. 3 IEA), writings, words printed/lithographed/photographed, maps/plans, inscriptions on metal plates/stones, and caricatures are expressly listed as illustrations of 'document'—'Private papers' is not listed among the statutory illustrations (note: also distinguish Sec. 74/75 public vs private documents).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Because writings on paper are documents in general usage, candidates hesitate to exclude 'Private papers', forgetting the exact statutory illustrations to 'Document'.
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize the exact 5 illustrations of 'Document' in Sec. 2(1)(d) BSA: Writing, Print/Photo, Map/Plan, Inscription, Caricature (+ electronic/digital records).

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.statuteRef: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Order IX Rule 2)
questions.question: As per the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, where the plaintiff in a civil suit fails to pay the requisite court fee or postal charges for service of summons within the time permitted by the court, the court may :

options.label: A
options.text: Stay the proceedings until service is effected.

options.label: B
options.text: Proceed to decide the suit on merits.

options.label: C
options.text: Return the plaint for fresh presentation.

options.label: D
options.text: Dismiss the suit.

rectification.principle: Order IX Rule 2 CPC provides that where on the day fixed it is found that the summons has not been served upon the defendant in consequence of the plaintiff's failure to pay the court-fee or postal charges for such service, the Court may make an order that the suit be dismissed.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates confuse Order IX Rule 2 (dismissal of suit for non-payment of summons process fee) with Order VII Rule 10 (return of plaint for lack of jurisdiction).
rectification.howToRectify: Order IX Rule 2 CPC = Failure to pay court-fee/postal charges for summons -> Court may dismiss the suit (fresh suit allowed under Order IX Rule 4).

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.statuteRef: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (Sec. 7 Proviso)
questions.question: Under the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, which situation makes the consent of a wife unnecessary for adoption ?

options.label: A
options.text: She has ceased to be a Hindu by conversion.

options.label: B
options.text: She refuses consent due to personal disagreement.

options.label: C
options.text: She is living separately without legal separation.

options.label: D
options.text: None of the above

rectification.principle: Under the proviso to Section 7 of HAMA, 1956, a male Hindu must obtain his wife's consent to adopt unless she has completely and finally renounced the world, or has ceased to be a Hindu, or has been declared by a court of competent jurisdiction to be of unsound mind.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Mere living separately without divorce/judicial separation or personal disagreement does NOT dispense with the wife's consent.
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize the 3 exceptions in Sec. 7 proviso HAMA: (1) Renounced world, (2) Ceased to be Hindu, (3) Unsound mind declared by Court.
